description: Farming spread (spec neolithic/farming-spread.md): dated waypoints where farming or herding arrived, and the speed parameters of the wave that fills the gaps between them. Years are 'bce'; a negative bce is a year CE (-1000 is 1000 CE).

seaMaxHopKm.note: Farthest open-water jump a wave makes (Tonga to Samoa about 800 km); beyond it only waypoints and holds carry farming.
seaMaxHopKm.source: derived from the Lapita and Cardial waypoints of this file

zones.source: Pinhasi, Fort & Ammerman 2005, PLoS Biology 3(12): 0.6-1.3 km/yr (95%); Fort 2015, J. R. Soc. Interface 12: about 1 km/yr

zones.note: Applies to sea hops and the 50 km coastal strip of the Mediterranean and Black Sea. The Cardial rate of 5 km/yr holds for the western Mediterranean alone; over the whole sea, with the pauses of section 9.3, 1.5 km/yr fits the dated waypoints.
zones.source: Zilhao 2001, PNAS 98 (Cardial about 5 km/yr); Isern et al. 2017, PNAS 114

zones.note: Open water runs at this speed only inside the box (the Austronesian and Lapita seas); other water runs at the speed of the land zone around it.

default.note: Used where no zone box matches.

The Anatolian pause: farming stood in central Anatolia from about 8200 BCE yet crossed the Aegean only about 6700 BCE; Weninger et al. 2014, Documenta Praehistorica 41; Özdoğan 2011, Current Anthropology 52 S4
Khvalynsk herders on the middle and lower Volga kept cattle and sheep by about 4500 BCE; Anthony 2007, The Horse, the Wheel and Language
Cattle and sheep reached the Azov and Dnieper steppes about 5500 to 5000 BCE (Dnieper-Donets II); Anthony 2007, The Horse, the Wheel and Language
Farming reached the far eastern steppe (Kazakhstan, Botai foragers) only about 3800 BCE; Anthony 2007, The Horse, the Wheel and Language
Starčevo-Criş farmers reached Moldavia and the Carpathian foothills about 5800 to 5500 BCE, before Cucuteni-Trypillia (about 5100); Reingruber & Thissen 2009, Radiocarbon 51
Shulaveri-Shomu farming begins about 5800 BCE; Hamon 2008
The Iranian desert plateau slowed the eastward spread; Jeitun farming about 6400 BCE; Harris 2010, Origins of Agriculture in Western Central Asia
Neolithic farming reaches Egypt and the Sahara about 5500 BCE; Wengrow et al. 2014, Antiquity 88; Dunne et al. 2012, Nature 486
Impressa and Cardial farming begin about 5900 BCE in the central and western Mediterranean; Zilhão 2001, PNAS 98
Millet farming of the Chulmun period from about 3500 BCE, rice and intensive fields of the Mumun period from about 1500 BCE; Crawford & Lee 2003, Antiquity 77; Lee 2011, Current Anthropology 52 S4
Yayoi rice farming reaches Kinki and Tohoku after Kyushu; Hudson 1999; Mizoguchi 2013
The Ryukyu islands had farming villages only from the Gusuku period, about 900 to 1100 CE; Pearson 2013, Okinawa: The Rise of an Island Kingdom
Hokkaido stayed with the foraging Epi-Jomon until the farming Satsumon culture, about 700 CE; Mizoguchi 2013, The Archaeology of Japan
Dabenkeng farming of rice and millet, about 3600 BCE; Bellwood 2005; Tsang 2005
Rice farming reaches mainland South-East Asia about 2300 BCE; Higham 2002; Bellwood 2005
Austronesian farmers reach Luzon about 2300 BCE; Bellwood 2005; Hung et al. 2011
Farming in the islands between Asia and New Guinea begins about 1600 BCE; Bellwood 2005; Spriggs 2011
Southern Neolithic of the Deccan, about 3200 BCE; Fuller 2011, Rice 4
Millet farmers reach the Tibetan plateau edge about 3500 BCE; d'Alpoim Guedes 2015
Cultivation reaches Finland about 2600 BCE; Sørensen & Karg 2014, J. Archaeol. Sci. 51
Maize farming of the Maya lowlands, about 2900 BCE; Pohl et al. 1996, Science 274; Smith 1998
Farming on the Titicaca altiplano, about 2100 BCE; Bruno 2014
Maize arrives in the Eastern Woodlands only about 150 CE; Hart & Lovis 2013, J. Archaeol. Res. 21
Yayoi rice farming begins in northern Kyushu about 1000 BCE; Hudson 1999; Mizoguchi 2013
Starčevo and Körös farming begin about 6200 BCE; Reingruber & Thissen 2009, Radiocarbon 51
Coastal Peru farming of squash, beans and cotton, about 3200 BCE; Shady et al. 2001, Science 292
Maize reaches the American Southwest about 2300 BCE; Merrill et al. 2009, PNAS 106
Farming villages on the Antilles, about 500 BCE; Rouse 1992; Keegan 2013
Farming villages on the Antilles, about 500 BCE; Rouse 1992; Keegan 2013
Southern Brazil highland farming, about 100 BCE; Iriarte et al. 2013, Quaternary International
Pearl millet farming of the western Sahel, about 2400 BCE; Manning et al. 2011, J. Archaeol. Sci. 38
Yam and oil-palm farming of the Guinea forest edge, about 1900 BCE; Neumann et al. 2012
Pastoralists reach the Turkana basin about 3500 BCE; Ambrose 1998; Lane 2013
Ensete, teff and cattle in the Ethiopian highlands, about 3000 BCE; Brandt 1984; Harlan 1992
Pastoral Neolithic of the Kenya Rift, about 1500 BCE; Ambrose 1998
Urewe farmers with iron about 800 BCE; Schmidt 1997
Bantu-speaking farmers leave the Cameroon grassfields about 1500 BCE; Grollemund et al. 2015, PNAS 112
Early Iron Age farmers reach the Limpopo about 100 BCE; Huffman 2007
The Ertebølle foragers of southern Scandinavia kept their way of life until about 3950 BCE; Sørensen & Karg 2014, J. Archaeol. Sci. 51

noFarming.source: Hunter-gatherers to 1991 CE; Torres Strait gardens are the only exception (Bellwood 2005)

barriers.source: No Old World crop crossed the Bering Strait before 1492 CE; American farming began on its own (Bellwood 2005, First Farmers; Larson et al. 2014, PNAS 111)
Same: open water of the North Pacific and the Bering Strait stops the wave
